sections.md:
- **Messaging**: Kafka (`rdkafka`), NATS, RabbitMQ (`lapin`). Consumers must be idempotent; commit offsets after the work succeeds; park poison messages in a dead-letter topic.
- **Observability**: the `tracing` crate gives structured logs *and* spans; `tracing-subscriber` formats them (JSON in production) and `tracing-opentelemetry` exports traces. Expose Prometheus metrics (`metrics`, `axum-prometheus`) and a `/healthz` endpoint.
- **Configuration**: twelve-factor style: environment variables or files loaded with `figment` / `config` into a typed struct, validated at startup, secrets never logged.
- **Auth**: verify JWT signatures and expiry (`jsonwebtoken`), hash passwords with `argon2`, and put authorisation in middleware.
- **Graceful shutdown**: listen for SIGTERM, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, then close pools.

sections.title: Quality Gates & CI
sections.md:
Make the toolchain enforce the standard on every pull request:

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check          # formatting
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings   # lints as errors
cargo test --all --locked           # unit + integration tests, exact lockfile
cargo doc --no-deps                 # docs must build
cargo audit                         # known vulnerabilities (RustSec)
cargo deny check                    # licences, bans, duplicate versions
```

- Commit `Cargo.lock` for applications and use `--locked` in CI for reproducible builds.
- Use a **workspace** to split a project into crates that compile and test independently; use **feature flags** to make heavy dependencies optional.
- Cache `~/.cargo` and `target/` in CI (for example with `Swatinem/rust-cache`) to keep builds fast.
- Follow semantic versioning for libraries and declare a minimum supported Rust version (MSRV).

sections.title: Build, Deploy & Debug
sections.md:
- **Release profile**: `lto`, `codegen-units = 1`, `strip = true`; consider `panic = "abort"` when you do not need unwinding.
- **Containers**: a multi-stage Dockerfile builds in a full Rust image and copies only the binary into a slim or distroless image. For fully static binaries target `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` (use `rustls` instead of OpenSSL).
- **Cross-compiling** with `cross` or `cargo zigbuild`; keep debug symbols in separate files for post-mortem debugging.
- **Debugging**: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` for panic traces, `gdb`/`lldb` (`rust-gdb`) for live and core-dump inspection, `tokio-console` for stuck or slow async tasks, `cargo flamegraph` for CPU hot spots, `heaptrack` or `dhat` for allocations.
- **Deploy safely**: health and readiness probes, rolling or blue-green releases, canary a percentage of traffic, keep a one-command rollback, and write a runbook for the failure modes below.

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two different elements whose values add up to `target`. Exactly one valid pair exists, and you may return the indices in any order.
questions.approach: Store each value's index in a `HashMap` as you scan. For the current number, look up `target - n`; if it was seen earlier you have the pair. One pass, constant-time lookups.

questions.title: Contains Duplicate
questions.statement: Return `true` if any value appears at least twice in the array, otherwise `false`.
questions.approach: `HashSet::insert` returns `false` when the value is already present, so the first failed insert is a duplicate. Sorting would give O(1) extra space at O(N log N) time.

questions.title: Valid Anagram
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Fixed size array `int[26]`)
questions.statement: Given two strings `s` and `t` of lowercase letters, return `true` if `t` is a rearrangement of the letters of `s`.
questions.approach: Count letters of `s` up and letters of `t` down in one `[i32; 26]`. If the lengths match and every count ends at zero, they are anagrams. Constant space because the alphabet is fixed.

questions.title: Group Anagrams
questions.target: O(N · K) Time, O(N · K) Space
questions.statement: Group the strings in `strs` so that every group contains words that are anagrams of each other. Groups and the words inside them may be returned in any order.
questions.approach: Anagrams share the same letter-count signature. Use that signature (an array of 26 counts, which is `Hash`) as the map key, then push each word into its bucket. Sorting the letters of each word also works but costs O(K log K).

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.target: O(N) Time via Bucket Sort or O(N log K) via Min-Heap
questions.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` values that occur most often. The answer may be returned in any order, and it is guaranteed to be unique.
questions.approach: Count frequencies in a map, then bucket values by frequency (index = count, at most N). Walk the buckets from the highest frequency down until you have `k` values. That is O(N) with no sorting; a `BinaryHeap` of size `k` is the O(N log K) alternative.

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Prefix & Suffix products)
questions.statement: Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`. Do not use division and run in O(N).
questions.approach: Two passes. First fill `answer[i]` with the product of everything to the left of `i`. Then sweep right-to-left, multiplying by a running product of everything to the right. The output vector is the only storage, so auxiliary space is O(1).

questions.title: Valid Sudoku
questions.statement: Decide whether a partially filled 9x9 Sudoku board is valid. Only filled cells are checked: no digit may repeat in a row, a column, or any of the nine 3x3 boxes. Empty cells are `'.'`. The board does not need to be solvable.

tests.input: The same board but the first row is "83..7...." (two 8s in column 0)

questions.approach: Walk all 81 cells once and record each digit together with its row, column and box in a `HashSet` of tuples. A failed `insert` means a repeat. The board size is fixed, so time and space are O(1).

questions.title: Encode and Decode Strings
questions.statement: Design `encode` and `decode` so a list of strings can be turned into one string and recovered exactly. The strings may contain any characters, including your delimiter.

tests.output: encoded "4#lint4#code4#love3#you", decoded back to the same list

questions.approach: Prefix every string with its byte length and a `#`. When decoding, read the number up to the next `#`, then take exactly that many bytes. Because you always skip by length, a `#` inside the data is harmless.

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(N) Space (`HashSet` boundary lookup)
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (such as 4,5,6,7) that can be formed from the values of `nums`, in any order. It must run in O(N).
questions.approach: Put every value in a `HashSet`. Only start counting from numbers that have no predecessor (`n - 1` absent); from there walk upward while `n + 1` exists. Each element is visited a constant number of times.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.statement: Count the contiguous, non-empty subarrays of `nums` whose elements sum to `k`. Values can be negative, so a sliding window will not work.
questions.approach: Keep a running prefix sum and a map of how many times each prefix sum has occurred. A subarray ending here sums to `k` exactly when an earlier prefix equals `sum - k`, so add that count to the answer. Seed the map with `0 -> 1`.

questions.title: Sort Colors (75 Ball Sort)
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Dutch National Flag algorithm)
questions.statement: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in place (red, white, blue) in one pass, without using a library sort.
questions.approach: Dutch National Flag: keep `lo` (next spot for 0), `hi` (next spot for 2) and a scanner `i`. Swap 0s to the front and 2s to the back; do not advance `i` after swapping with `hi`, because the swapped-in value is unchecked.

questions.title: Majority Element
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm)
questions.statement: Return the element that appears more than N/2 times in the array. A majority element is guaranteed to exist.
questions.approach: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter. Matching values increment it, others decrement it, and at zero the next value becomes the candidate. A true majority outvotes everything else combined, so it survives. O(1) space.

questions.title: Valid Palindrome
questions.statement: A phrase is a palindrome if, after lowercasing it and removing every character that is not a letter or digit, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Return whether string `s` is a palindrome.

tests.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

questions.approach: Two indices from both ends. Skip non-alphanumeric bytes on each side, compare the lowercase bytes, and move inward. No extra string is built, so space is O(1).

questions.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
questions.statement: `numbers` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the 1-based indices `[i, j]` (with `i < j`) of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one solution exists and you may not reuse an element. Use only constant extra space.
questions.approach: Start one index at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left index right; if too large, move the right index left. Sorting guarantees each move rules out a whole row of pairs.

questions.title: 3Sum
questions.target: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Sorting + Two Pointers)
questions.statement: Return all unique triplets `[a, b, c]` from `nums` such that `a + b + c == 0`. The result must not contain duplicate triplets.
questions.approach: Sort the vector. Fix the first value `nums[i]`, then solve a two-sum with two indices on the rest. Skip repeated values for `i`, `l` and `r` so no duplicate triplet is produced.

questions.title: Container With Most Water
questions.statement: `height[i]` is the height of a vertical line at position `i`. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water, and return that maximum area.
questions.approach: Start with the widest container (both ends). The area is limited by the shorter line, so moving the taller line can never help; move the shorter one inward and keep the best area seen.

questions.title: Trapping Rain Water
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Two Pointers / Two Arrays)
questions.statement: `height` describes an elevation map where each bar has width 1. After it rains, return how many units of water are trapped between the bars.
questions.approach: Water above a bar equals the lower of the tallest bars on its left and right, minus its own height. Two indices track the running left max and right max; always process the side with the smaller bar, since its limit is already known.

questions.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
questions.statement: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place so each value appears once, keeping the relative order. Return `k`, the number of unique values; the first `k` slots must hold them.
questions.approach: A write index marks where the next unique value goes; a scanning index walks the vector. Whenever the scanned value differs from the last kept one, copy it to the write position.

questions.title: Move Zeroes
questions.statement: Move every `0` in the array to the end while keeping the order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place.
questions.approach: Keep a write index for the next non-zero value. Scan the vector, swapping each non-zero element into the write position. Zeros are pushed back automatically.

questions.title: BackSpace String Compare
questions.statement: Both strings are typed into editors where `#` acts as a backspace (it does nothing on empty text). Return whether the two strings end up equal.
questions.approach: Walk both strings from the end. For each, skip characters that are cancelled by a `#` (count pending backspaces), then compare the next real bytes. No stacks or rebuilt strings, so O(1) space.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.statement: `prices[i]` is a stock price on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit, and return that profit (0 if no profit is possible).
questions.approach: Track the lowest price seen so far. For each day, the best profit selling today is `price - min_price`. Keep the maximum. One pass, O(1) space.

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest substring of `s` that contains no repeated character.
questions.approach: Sliding window with a table of each byte's last seen index. When a character repeats inside the window, jump the window start just past its previous position. The window always holds unique characters.

questions.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
questions.statement: You may change at most `k` characters of uppercase string `s` to any other letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of one repeated letter.
questions.approach: Keep a window and the count of its most frequent letter. The window is valid while `length - max_count <= k` (the rest can be replaced). Otherwise slide the left edge. The max count never needs to shrink, because only a larger count can improve the answer.

questions.title: Permutation in String
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Fixed window size array matching)
questions.statement: Return `true` if `s2` contains a substring that is a permutation of `s1`.
questions.approach: Slide a fixed window of length `s1.len()` over `s2`, maintaining letter counts for the window and comparing with the counts of `s1`. Adding the new letter and removing the old one is O(1) per step.

questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
questions.statement: Return the smallest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t` (including duplicates). If none exists, return an empty string.
questions.approach: Expand the right edge until the window covers all of `t` (tracked with a `missing` counter and a need table). Then shrink from the left while it still covers everything, recording the best window each time.

questions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(K) Space (`ArrayDeque` monotonic queue)
questions.statement: A window of size `k` slides from the left of `nums` to the right, one position at a time. Return the maximum of each window position.
questions.approach: Keep a `VecDeque` of indices whose values are in decreasing order. Before adding index `i`, drop smaller values from the back (they can never be a max again) and drop the front if it left the window. The front is always the current maximum.

questions.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
questions.statement: Find the contiguous subarray of length exactly `k` with the largest average and return that average.
questions.approach: Compute the sum of the first `k` elements, then slide: add the new element, subtract the one leaving. Track the maximum sum and divide by `k` once at the end.

questions.title: Valid Parentheses
questions.statement: `s` contains only the characters `()[]{}`. Return whether every bracket is closed by the same type, in the correct order.
questions.approach: Push the closing bracket you expect for every opening bracket. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must equal it. At the end the stack must be empty.

questions.title: Min Stack
questions.statement: Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top` and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.
questions.approach: Keep a second stack of running minimums. Every push also pushes `min(value, current_min)`; every pop removes from both. The top of the min stack is always the current minimum.

questions.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
questions.statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression given in Reverse Polish Notation. Operators are `+ - * /`; division truncates toward zero. Every intermediate result fits in 32 bits.
questions.approach: Scan the tokens with a stack. Numbers are pushed; an operator pops the top two values (right operand first), applies the operation and pushes the result. The last value left is the answer. Integer division in Rust already truncates toward zero.

questions.title: Generate Parentheses
questions.statement: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, generate every combination of well-formed parentheses.
questions.approach: Backtracking. You can add `(` while fewer than `n` have been used, and `)` only while it would not exceed the number of opens. Every path that reaches length `2n` is valid. Push and pop on one `String` to avoid allocating at every step.

questions.title: Daily Temperatures
questions.statement: For each day, return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature. If no warmer day follows, the answer for that day is 0.
questions.approach: Monotonic stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. When today is warmer than the temperature at the top index, that earlier day has found its answer (`today - index`); pop and repeat.

questions.title: Car Fleet
questions.target: O(N log N) Time, O(N) Space
questions.statement: Cars at the given `position`s drive toward `target` at their own `speed`. A faster car that catches a slower one must slow down and drive bumper to bumper, forming a fleet. Return the number of fleets that arrive at the target.
questions.approach: Sort cars by position, closest to the target first, and compute each car's arrival time. If a car would arrive later than the fleet ahead of it, it is a new fleet; otherwise it merges into that fleet.

questions.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
questions.statement: `heights[i]` is the height of a histogram bar of width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.
questions.approach: Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars: each popped bar's rectangle extends from the new stack top to the current index. A sentinel height of 0 at the end flushes the stack.

questions.title: Binary Search
questions.statement: `nums` is sorted ascending with distinct values. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if it is absent, in O(log N).
questions.approach: Keep a half-open range `[lo, hi)`. Compare the middle element with the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. Compute `mid` as `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`; with `usize` bounds a half-open range also avoids underflow.

questions.title: Search a 2D Matrix
questions.statement: Each row of the matrix is sorted, and the first number of a row is greater than the last number of the previous row. Return whether `target` is in the matrix, in O(log(M·N)).
questions.approach: The matrix behaves like one sorted array of `rows * cols` elements. Binary search over the virtual index and convert with `row = mid / cols`, `col = mid % cols`.

questions.title: Koko Eating Bananas
questions.target: O(N log(max P)) Binary Search on Answer
questions.statement: Koko has `h` hours to eat all banana piles. At speed `k` bananas/hour she eats from one pile per hour (finishing a smaller pile wastes the rest of that hour). Return the minimum integer `k` that lets her finish within `h` hours.
questions.approach: Binary search on the answer `k` between 1 and the largest pile. For a candidate `k`, the hours needed are the sum of `ceil(pile / k)`. Feasibility is monotonic, so find the smallest feasible `k`.

questions.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.statement: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (for example `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` became `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`). Return the minimum element in O(log N).
questions.approach: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`. If mid is larger, the minimum is to its right; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Narrow until the bounds meet.

questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.statement: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if it is not present, in O(log N).
questions.approach: At every step one half around `mid` is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half; if so search it, otherwise search the other half. Signed indices keep `mid - 1` safe at zero.

questions.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
questions.target: O(log N) Get, O(1) Set (`TreeMap` or `ArrayList` binary search)
questions.statement: Design a key-value store where each key keeps multiple values with increasing timestamps. `set(key, value, timestamp)` stores a value; `get(key, timestamp)` returns the value whose timestamp is the largest one not greater than the query, or an empty string if none exists.
questions.approach: Store a `BTreeMap<i32, String>` per key and use `range(..=timestamp).next_back()` for the lookup, which is O(log N). With strictly increasing timestamps a `Vec` plus manual binary search gives O(1) set.

questions.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.statement: Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return the median of all their elements combined. The running time must be O(log(min(M, N))).
questions.approach: Binary search a partition of the shorter vector so that the left halves of both together hold half the elements and every left value is at most every right value. Then the median comes from the four values around the cut.

questions.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
questions.statement: In a sorted array, return the `[first, last]` indices of `target`, or `[-1,-1]` if it does not occur. It must run in O(log N).
questions.approach: Run a binary search twice: once for the first index whose value is at least `target`, and once for the first index whose value is strictly greater. The range is `[first, first_greater - 1]`, valid only if the first position holds the target.

questions.title: Reverse Linked List
questions.statement: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
questions.approach: Walk the list once, taking each node out of its place (`take()` leaves `None` behind) and pointing it at the node before it. Ownership moves along with the nodes, so no `unsafe` is needed. O(1) extra space.

questions.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
questions.statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list made from the nodes of both, and return its head.
questions.approach: Use a dummy head and a `tail` reference. Repeatedly detach the smaller front node of the two lists and append it. When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other.

questions.title: Reorder List
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Find middle, reverse 2nd half, merge)
questions.statement: Reorder a list `L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln` in place into `L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> ...`. You may not change node values, only the links.
questions.approach: Three steps: find the middle by counting nodes, split off and reverse the second half, then interleave the two halves node by node. Every node is moved, never copied, and no extra collection is built.

questions.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.statement: Remove the `n`-th node from the end of a list and return the head.
questions.approach: Count the nodes, then walk to the node just before the one to delete and splice it out with `take()`. A dummy head handles removing the first node. (A fast/slow pointer pair is awkward under Rust's single mutable borrow, so two passes are the idiomatic choice.)

questions.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space (Interleaving nodes)
questions.statement: A linked list is stored in an arena `Vec<Node>`. Each node has a value, a `next` index and a `random` index (any node, or none). Given the arena and the index of the head, return a deep copy: a new arena holding only the nodes reachable from the head, laid out in list order (the head at index 0), with `next` and `random` rewritten to the new indices.

tests.output: new arena with the same values and links (7, 13, 11 at indices 0, 1, 2)

tests.input: nodes: 11, 13, 7 stored out of order, head = 7
tests.output: new arena in list order: 7, 13, 11 with every index translated

questions.approach: Safe Rust cannot hold aliasing pointers, so nodes refer to each other by index. Pass 1 walks the list and records `old index -> new index` in a `HashMap`. Pass 2 copies each node, translating `next` and `random` through that map.

questions.title: Add Two Numbers
questions.statement: Two non-empty lists store non-negative integers with the digits in reverse order (least significant digit first). Add the numbers and return the sum in the same format.
questions.approach: Add digit by digit like grade-school addition, carrying into the next node. Keep going while either list has digits or a carry remains, treating missing digits as 0.

questions.title: Linked List Cycle
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
questions.statement: A singly linked list is stored as a vector: `next[i]` is the index of the node after node `i`, or `-1` if node `i` is the tail. The head is node 0 (an empty vector is an empty list). Return whether the list contains a cycle.
questions.approach: Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one index by 1 and another by 2. If there is a cycle the fast index eventually laps the slow one; otherwise it reaches the `-1` tail. (A cycle cannot be built from owning `Box` nodes, which is why the list is index-based here.)

questions.title: Linked List Cycle II
questions.statement: A singly linked list is stored as a vector: `next[i]` is the index of the node after node `i`, or `-1` for the tail; the head is node 0. If the list has a cycle, return the index of the node where the cycle begins, otherwise `-1`.
questions.approach: Use Floyd's algorithm to detect a meeting point. Then restart one index from the head and move both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the cycle entrance, because the distance from the head to the entrance equals the distance from the meeting point to it around the loop.

questions.title: Find the Duplicate Number
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (Floyd's cycle on array indices)
questions.statement: `nums` has `n + 1` integers, each between 1 and `n`, and exactly one value is repeated (possibly many times). Return the repeated value without modifying the array and using only O(1) extra space.
questions.approach: Treat `i -> nums[i]` as a linked list. A duplicate means two indices point to the same next node, so the list has a cycle and the duplicate value is the cycle entrance. Find it with Floyd's two phases; the vector is never modified.

questions.title: LRU Cache
questions.target: O(1) Get & Put (`HashMap` + Doubly Linked List)
questions.statement: Design a Least Recently Used cache with a fixed capacity. `get(key)` returns the value or -1; `put(key, value)` inserts or updates and evicts the least recently used key when the capacity is exceeded. Both must run in O(1).
questions.approach: A `HashMap` gives O(1) lookup of nodes; a doubly linked list keeps usage order (most recent at the front). Safe Rust cannot hold two owning pointers per node, so the list lives in a `Vec` arena and nodes link by index; evicted slots are recycled through a free list. Every access moves the node to the front; eviction removes the node before the tail sentinel.

questions.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
questions.statement: Merge `k` sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and return it.
questions.approach: Keep a min-heap (`BinaryHeap` of `Reverse`) holding the current head of each list. Pop the smallest, append that node to the result, and push its successor. Each of the N nodes costs O(log K).

questions.title: Invert Binary Tree
questions.statement: Invert a binary tree (swap the left and right child of every node) and return its root.
questions.approach: Take the two children out of the node (`take()`), invert each subtree recursively, and put them back swapped. Every node is visited once; the call stack depth equals the tree height. The tree is owned, so it is rebuilt in place with no cloning.

questions.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
questions.approach: The depth of a node is 1 plus the larger depth of its two subtrees; an empty tree has depth 0. The tree is only read, so it is borrowed (`&Option<Box<TreeNode>>`).

questions.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return the diameter of a binary tree: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root.
questions.approach: For each node, the longest path through it is `height(left) + height(right)`. Compute heights bottom-up in one DFS and update a best-so-far value (passed as `&mut`) as you go.

questions.title: Balanced Binary Tree
questions.statement: Return whether a binary tree is height-balanced: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
questions.approach: Compute heights bottom-up and return -1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced, so each node is processed once instead of recomputing heights at every level.

questions.title: Same Tree
questions.statement: Return whether two binary trees are identical: same shape and same node values.
questions.approach: Compare roots, then recurse on both left children and both right children. Matching on the pair `(p, q)` handles all four cases: two empty trees match, one empty and one not does not.

questions.title: Subtree of Another Tree
questions.statement: Return whether `subRoot` appears as a subtree of `root`: some node of `root` has exactly the same structure and values as `subRoot` (including all of that node's descendants).
questions.approach: For every node in `root`, check whether the tree rooted there is identical to `sub_root` using a same-tree comparison. Worst case O(N · M).

questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
questions.statement: In a binary search tree, return the value of the lowest common ancestor of the two nodes holding the values `p` and `q`: the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as a descendant of itself). Both values are in the tree.
questions.approach: Use the BST ordering. If both values are smaller than the current node, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is where the paths split, so it is the LCA. Iterative, O(H), walking down with shared references.

questions.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.statement: Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree: a list of lists, where each inner list holds one level's values from left to right.
questions.approach: Breadth-first search with a `VecDeque`. Process exactly `queue.len()` nodes per round so each round is one level, pushing children for the next round.

questions.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
questions.statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, from top to bottom.
questions.approach: Level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one visible from the right. A DFS visiting the right child first and recording the first node at each depth also works.

questions.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
questions.statement: A node `X` is "good" if no node on the path from the root to `X` has a value greater than `X`. Return the number of good nodes in the tree.
questions.approach: DFS carrying the maximum value seen on the path so far. A node is good when its value is at least that maximum; then pass the updated maximum to its children.

questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
questions.statement: Return whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger (strictly).
questions.approach: Pass down an allowed `(min, max)` range. Each node must lie strictly inside it; going left tightens the max, going right tightens the min. Checking only direct children is not enough (see the third case). Use `i64` bounds so `std::i32::MIN` and `std::i32::MAX` nodes work.

questions.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.statement: Return the `k`-th smallest value (1-indexed) in a binary search tree.
questions.approach: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order. Walk it iteratively with a stack of references and stop at the `k`-th node, which costs O(H + K).

questions.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.statement: Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree with unique values, rebuild and return the tree.
questions.approach: The first preorder value is the root. Its position in the inorder sequence splits left and right subtrees. A map from value to inorder index gives O(1) splits, and a moving preorder cursor picks each next root.

questions.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.statement: A path in a binary tree is any sequence of connected nodes, going through each node at most once, and it need not pass through the root. Return the maximum sum of node values over all non-empty paths.
questions.approach: For each node compute the best downward path starting there (`node + max(0, left, right)`). The best path bending at the node is `node + max(0, left) + max(0, right)`; track the global maximum. Negative branches are ignored.

questions.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.statement: Design `serialize` and `deserialize` for a binary tree: convert the tree to a string and rebuild exactly the same tree from that string. You choose the format.
questions.approach: Pre-order DFS, writing `#` for empty children. Because pre-order plus explicit empties is unambiguous, deserialization consumes the tokens in the same order and rebuilds recursively from a single iterator.

questions.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
questions.target: O(L) Insert/Search where L is word length
questions.statement: Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with `insert(word)`, `search(word)` (exact match) and `startsWith(prefix)`. All input is lowercase letters.
questions.approach: Each node holds 26 optional child links and an `is_word` flag. Every operation walks one node per byte, so it costs O(L) for a word of length L. `get_or_insert_with` creates missing children on the way down.

questions.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.statement: Design a data structure supporting `addWord(word)` and `search(pattern)`, where the pattern may contain `.` that matches any single letter.
questions.approach: Store words in a trie. For a normal letter follow one child; for `.` try every child recursively (DFS). Worst case grows with the number of wildcards, but ordinary lookups stay O(L).

questions.title: Word Search II
questions.statement: Given a grid of letters and a list of words, return every word that can be traced in the grid through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per word.
questions.approach: Put all words in a trie, then DFS from every cell while walking the trie. A branch with no matching trie child is abandoned immediately, which prunes most of the search. Take the word out of its node once found to avoid duplicates, and mark visited cells in place.

questions.title: Subsets
questions.statement: Return all subsets (the power set) of an array of distinct integers. The result must not contain duplicate subsets; any order is accepted.
questions.approach: Backtracking: at each step record the current subset, then try adding each later element, recurse, and remove it with `pop`. Choosing only from indices after the last pick prevents duplicates. There are 2^N subsets.

questions.title: Combination Sum
questions.statement: Given distinct positive integers `candidates` and a `target`, return every unique combination whose numbers sum to `target`. Each number may be used any number of times.
questions.approach: Backtrack with a start index. Reusing the same number means recursing with `i` (not `i + 1`); moving the start forward avoids permutations of the same combination. Stop when the remaining amount hits 0.

questions.title: Permutations
questions.statement: Return all permutations of an array of distinct integers, in any order.
questions.approach: Build each permutation position by position, choosing any value not yet used (tracked with a `Vec<bool>`), recursing, then un-choosing. N! results of length N.

questions.title: Subsets II
questions.statement: `nums` may contain duplicates. Return all possible subsets without duplicate subsets, in any order.
questions.approach: Sort first so equal values are adjacent. In the loop, skip `nums[i]` when it equals `nums[i-1]` and `i > start`: that value was already tried at this depth, so using it again would repeat a subset.

questions.title: Word Search
questions.statement: Return whether `word` can be built by walking through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells of the grid, never using the same cell twice.
questions.approach: DFS from every cell that matches the first letter. Mark the current cell as used while exploring its four neighbours, then restore it when backtracking.

questions.title: Palindrome Partitioning
questions.statement: Partition string `s` so that every piece is a palindrome, and return all possible partitionings.
questions.approach: Backtracking over cut positions: from the current start, try every end index; if `s[start..=end]` is a palindrome, take it and recurse on the rest. When the start reaches the end of the string, record the partition.

questions.title: N-Queens
questions.statement: Place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Return every distinct arrangement as a list of board strings using `'Q'` and `'.'`.
questions.approach: Place one queen per row, trying each column. Track used columns and both diagonals in boolean vectors (`row - col` and `row + col` identify diagonals) so each check is O(1). Backtrack when no column is free.

questions.title: Number of Islands
questions.statement: The grid contains `'1'` (land) and `'0'` (water). Return the number of islands, where an island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically.
questions.approach: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill (DFS) all connected land, sinking it to `'0'` so it is not counted again. The grid is passed as `&mut` to the helper, so the sinking needs no extra visited array.

questions.title: Clone Graph
questions.statement: Given a reference to a node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph. Each node has an integer value and a list of neighbours.

tests.output: a new graph with the same shape and values (no shared nodes)

questions.approach: DFS with a map from original value to its clone. If a node was already cloned, return the existing clone; this also breaks cycles. Otherwise create the clone, register it, then clone each neighbour. Shared, cyclic graphs need `Rc<RefCell<…>>`; a cycle of `Rc`s is never freed, which is the classic caveat (use `Weak` for back edges in real code).

questions.title: Max Area of Island
questions.statement: In a binary grid, an island is a group of `1`s connected horizontally or vertically. Return the area (number of cells) of the largest island, or 0 if there is none.
questions.approach: DFS from every land cell, returning 1 plus the areas of its four neighbours and sinking each visited cell to 0. Track the largest area returned.

questions.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
questions.target: O(M · N) Time (Reverse DFS from oceans)
questions.statement: `heights[r][c]` is the height of a cell. The Pacific Ocean touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Water flows to neighbouring cells of equal or lower height. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.
questions.approach: Run the search in reverse: start from the ocean borders and climb to neighbours that are equal or higher. Do this once for each ocean, then keep the cells reached by both.

questions.title: Surrounded Regions
questions.statement: A board contains `'X'` and `'O'`. Capture every region of `'O'` that is completely surrounded by `'X'` by flipping its cells to `'X'`. An `'O'` on the border, or connected to one, is not captured.
questions.approach: Work backwards from the border: mark every `'O'` reachable from a border `'O'` as safe (`'T'`). Then flip the remaining `'O'` to `'X'` and turn `'T'` back to `'O'`.

questions.title: Rotting Oranges
questions.statement: In a grid, `0` is empty, `1` is a fresh orange and `2` is a rotten orange. Every minute, each fresh orange next to a rotten one (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that is impossible.
questions.approach: Multi-source BFS: start with all rotten oranges in the queue and spread one level per minute, counting the fresh oranges that get infected. If any fresh orange is left at the end, return -1.

questions.title: Walls and Gates
questions.statement: A grid of rooms holds `-1` (wall), `0` (gate) and `2147483647` (empty room, "INF"). Fill each empty room with the number of steps to its nearest gate, or leave it as INF if no gate is reachable.
questions.approach: Multi-source BFS from every gate at once. The first time BFS reaches an empty room is by the shortest path, so assign `distance + 1` and enqueue it. Rooms never reached keep INF (`std::i32::MAX`).

questions.title: Course Schedule
questions.target: O(V + E) Time (Topological Sort / Kahn's Algorithm / Cycle DFS)
questions.statement: There are `numCourses` courses labelled `0..n-1`. Each pair `[a, b]` means you must take course `b` before course `a`. Return whether all courses can be finished.
questions.approach: This is cycle detection in a directed graph. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take courses with in-degree 0, "remove" them and reduce their dependents' in-degree. If every course gets taken, there is no cycle.

questions.title: Course Schedule II
questions.statement: Same setup as Course Schedule, but return one valid order in which to take all courses. If it is impossible, return an empty array.
questions.approach: Run Kahn's topological sort and record courses in the order they are taken. If fewer than `num_courses` were taken, a cycle exists and the answer is empty.

questions.title: Redundant Connection
questions.statement: A tree with `n` nodes had one extra edge added, creating a cycle. Given the edges, return the extra edge to remove so the graph becomes a tree again. If several answers exist, return the one that occurs last in the input.
questions.approach: Union-Find (disjoint set). Process edges in order; an edge whose endpoints already share a root would close a cycle, so it is the redundant one. Path compression keeps each operation near O(1).

questions.title: Word Ladder
questions.statement: Transform `beginWord` into `endWord` by changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in `wordList`. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence (including both ends), or 0 if no sequence exists.
questions.approach: Shortest path in an implicit graph, so use BFS. From each word, try replacing every position with each letter `a-z` and keep results found in the dictionary. Removing a word from the dictionary when it is queued doubles as the visited check. The BFS level at which `end_word` appears is the answer.

questions.title: Climbing Stairs
questions.statement: You climb a staircase of `n` steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
questions.approach: The ways to reach step `i` equal the ways to reach `i-1` plus the ways to reach `i-2` (the Fibonacci recurrence). Only the last two values are needed, so space is O(1).

questions.title: House Robber
questions.statement: Each house holds some money, and robbing two adjacent houses triggers an alarm. Return the maximum amount you can rob in one night.
questions.approach: At each house choose the better of skipping it (keep the previous best) or robbing it (value plus the best from two houses back). Two rolling variables are enough.

questions.title: House Robber II
questions.statement: The houses are arranged in a circle, so the first and last houses are adjacent. Return the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
questions.approach: Because the first and last houses cannot both be robbed, the answer is the better of two linear problems: houses `0..n-1` and houses `1..n`. Handle a single house separately.

questions.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
questions.target: O(N^2) Time, O(1) Space (Expand around center)
questions.statement: Return the longest palindromic substring of `s`.
questions.approach: Expand around every possible centre: each byte (odd length) and each gap between bytes (even length). Grow while both ends match and remember the longest span. O(N²) time, O(1) space. The input is treated as ASCII bytes; slicing a `&str` by byte offsets is only safe at character boundaries.

questions.title: Decode Ways
questions.statement: Letters are encoded as `A=1 ... Z=26`. Given a digit string `s`, return the number of ways to decode it into letters.
questions.approach: `dp[i]` is the number of ways to decode the first `i` characters. A single digit adds `dp[i-1]` if it is 1-9; a two-digit number 10-26 adds `dp[i-2]`. Keep only the last two values.

questions.title: Coin Change
questions.statement: Given coin denominations and a target `amount`, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made. You have unlimited coins of each kind.
questions.approach: Bottom-up DP: `dp[a]` is the minimum coins for amount `a`. For each amount try every coin: `dp[a] = min(dp[a - coin] + 1)`. Initialise with a value larger than any answer to mark unreachable amounts.

questions.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
questions.target: O(N log N) Time (Patience Sorting + Binary Search)
questions.statement: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums` (elements keep their order but need not be adjacent).
questions.approach: Patience sorting: keep `tails[k]`, the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length `k+1`. For each number, binary search the first tail that is at least it and replace that tail (or push). The length of `tails` is the answer.

questions.title: Word Break
questions.statement: Return whether string `s` can be split into a sequence of one or more words from the dictionary `wordDict`. Words may be reused.
questions.approach: `dp[i]` is true if the first `i` bytes can be segmented. For each `i`, look for a split point `j` where `dp[j]` is true and `s[j..i]` is a dictionary word. Put the dictionary in a `HashSet` for O(1) lookups.

questions.title: Single Number
questions.target: O(N) Time, O(1) Space (XOR property A ⊕ A = 0)
questions.statement: Every element appears twice except one. Find the element that appears once, in O(N) time and O(1) extra space.
questions.approach: XOR has two useful properties: `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a`. Folding XOR over every element cancels all pairs and leaves the single number.

questions.title: Number of 1 Bits
questions.statement: Return the number of `1` bits in the binary representation of the 32-bit integer `n` (its Hamming weight).
questions.approach: Brian Kernighan's trick: `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit. Count how many times you can do that before `n` becomes 0; the loop runs once per set bit. (`n` is a `u32`, so there is no sign to worry about; the standard library also offers `count_ones()`.)

questions.title: Reverse Integer
questions.target: O(log_10 N) Time (Overflow checking before multiplication)
questions.statement: Reverse the digits of a signed 32-bit integer. If the reversed value falls outside the 32-bit range, return 0. You may not use 64-bit integers.
questions.approach: Pop the last digit with `% 10` and push it onto the result with `* 10`. Use `checked_mul` and `checked_add`: they return `None` on overflow, so you can return 0 without needing a wider integer type.

antiPatterns.title: Calling `unwrap()` on Input You Do Not Control
antiPatterns.why: Any missing variable, malformed value or empty input turns into a panic that takes the whole thread (or process) down. `unwrap` is for situations that are provably impossible, not for I/O or user data.

antiPatterns.title: Cloning to Silence the Borrow Checker
antiPatterns.why: `.clone()` allocates and copies. Using it to make a compiler error disappear hides a design question (who should own this data?) and costs time and memory in loops. Most of the time the function only needs to read.

antiPatterns.title: Holding a `MutexGuard` Across `.await`
antiPatterns.why: The guard lives across a suspension point, so every other task that needs the lock blocks a runtime thread, and the future is not `Send`, which breaks `tokio::spawn`. Under load this becomes a stall or a deadlock.

antiPatterns.title: Blocking the Async Runtime
antiPatterns.why: Async runtimes multiplex many tasks onto a few threads. A blocking call freezes its thread, and with enough requests every worker is stuck, so unrelated endpoints time out.

antiPatterns.title: Unbounded Queues and Channels
antiPatterns.why: When the consumer is slower than the producer the queue grows until the process runs out of memory. There is no back-pressure, so the failure arrives late and far from its cause.

antiPatterns.title: Index Loops Instead of Iterators
antiPatterns.why: Manual indexing invites off-by-one and length-mismatch panics and forces a bounds check for every element. Iterator adaptors state the intent, stop at the shorter input, and let the optimiser vectorise.

antiPatterns.title: `Rc<RefCell<T>>` Everywhere
antiPatterns.why: `RefCell` moves the borrow checker's rules from compile time to run time, so aliasing mistakes become panics in production. Widespread `Rc<RefCell<_>>` usually means ownership was never designed.

antiPatterns.title: `&Vec<T>` and `&String` Parameters
antiPatterns.why: `&Vec<T>` and `&String` accept fewer inputs than `&[T]` and `&str` while offering nothing extra, and they force callers to allocate. Slices accept vectors, arrays and sub-ranges alike.

antiPatterns.title: `unsafe` Without a Safe Wrapper or Safety Argument
antiPatterns.why: This function is *safe* to call but is actually unsound: any caller can trigger undefined behaviour. Unsafe code must either check its preconditions or be marked `unsafe fn` so the obligation moves to the caller, and every block needs a documented invariant.

antiPatterns.title: Swallowing Errors with `let _ =`
antiPatterns.why: `Result` is `#[must_use]` precisely so failures are not ignored. Discarding it means the caller believes the data was saved when it may not have been, which is a silent data-loss bug.

antiMatrix.pattern: `Box<dyn Error>` in a library's public API
antiMatrix.cause: Callers cannot match on error kinds.
antiMatrix.fix: Return a typed error enum (`thiserror`).

antiMatrix.pattern: `panic!` for expected failures in a library
antiMatrix.cause: A bad input crashes the caller's process.
antiMatrix.fix: Return `Result`; reserve panics for bugs.

antiMatrix.pattern: `expect("")` with an empty or vague message
antiMatrix.cause: The failure gives no context in logs.
antiMatrix.fix: Describe the broken assumption, or add context with `anyhow`.

antiMatrix.cause: Errors cannot be matched, chained or localised.
antiMatrix.fix: Use typed errors that implement `std::error::Error` with `source()`.

antiMatrix.pattern: Cloning large structs inside hot loops
antiMatrix.cause: Hidden allocations and copies dominate runtime.
antiMatrix.fix: Borrow, use `Rc`/`Arc` or `Cow`, restructure the data flow.

antiMatrix.pattern: Self-referential structs built with raw tricks
antiMatrix.cause: Moves invalidate internal references (UB).
antiMatrix.fix: Store indices, use an arena, or `Pin` plus a vetted crate.

antiMatrix.cause: Memory is never freed; hides a design issue.
antiMatrix.fix: Restructure ownership, use `Arc`, or scoped threads.

antiMatrix.cause: Leaks locks, handles and memory.
antiMatrix.fix: Design a proper `Drop`, or use `ManuallyDrop` with care.

antiMatrix.cause: Values silently truncate or wrap.
antiMatrix.fix: Use `try_from` / `try_into` and handle the error.

antiMatrix.cause: `usize` underflow panics (debug) or wraps (release).
antiMatrix.fix: `checked_sub`, `saturating_sub` or `if let Some(last) = v.last()`.

antiMatrix.cause: Typos compile and fail at run time.
antiMatrix.fix: Model it as an `enum`.

antiMatrix.cause: Call sites are unreadable and easy to swap.
antiMatrix.fix: Use enums or a builder.

antiMatrix.pattern: Raw `u64` for every ID or unit
antiMatrix.cause: Different IDs or units get mixed up.
antiMatrix.fix: Newtype wrappers (`struct UserId(u64)`).

antiMatrix.cause: Every thread contends for a single lock.
antiMatrix.fix: Shard the map, use `RwLock` or `dashmap`, or message passing.

antiMatrix.cause: Two threads wait on each other forever.
antiMatrix.fix: Always lock in one global order, or merge into one lock.

antiMatrix.cause: Unbounded threads exhaust memory and the scheduler.
antiMatrix.fix: Use a bounded pool or async tasks.

antiMatrix.cause: One panic cascades into panics in every thread.
antiMatrix.fix: Handle `PoisonError` or use `parking_lot::Mutex`.

antiMatrix.cause: Other threads may never see the data the flag guards.
antiMatrix.fix: Use `Acquire`/`Release` (or `SeqCst`).

antiMatrix.pattern: Trying to share `Rc` across threads with `unsafe impl Send`
antiMatrix.cause: Non-atomic reference counts race: UB.
antiMatrix.fix: Use `Arc`.

antiMatrix.cause: Panics and errors in the task vanish silently.
antiMatrix.fix: Await or collect handles, log task results.

antiMatrix.cause: Dropped futures lose partially read data.
antiMatrix.fix: Use cancel-safe APIs or keep state outside the future.

antiMatrix.pattern: CPU-heavy work on the async runtime
antiMatrix.cause: Worker threads starve; latency spikes everywhere.
antiMatrix.fix: `spawn_blocking` or `rayon`.

antiMatrix.pattern: Huge arrays or buffers living across `.await`
antiMatrix.cause: Every future carries them: memory bloat, slow moves.
antiMatrix.fix: Box them or allocate on the heap.

antiMatrix.cause: One slow dependency hangs requests forever.
antiMatrix.fix: `tokio::time::timeout`, client-level timeouts.

antiMatrix.cause: Deploys drop in-flight requests.
antiMatrix.fix: Handle SIGTERM and drain (`with_graceful_shutdown`).

antiMatrix.pattern: `collect()` into a `Vec` only to iterate again
antiMatrix.cause: Needless allocation and a second pass.
antiMatrix.fix: Keep the iterator chain lazy.

antiMatrix.pattern: Building strings with `+` in a loop
antiMatrix.cause: Repeated reallocation and copying.
antiMatrix.fix: `push_str`, `write!`, `String::with_capacity`.

antiMatrix.cause: O(N) per operation makes loops O(N²).
antiMatrix.fix: Use `VecDeque`.

antiMatrix.cause: Repeated reallocation.
antiMatrix.fix: Reserve when the size is known.

antiMatrix.cause: Numbers are 10-100x off and misleading.
antiMatrix.fix: `--release` and `criterion`.

antiMatrix.pattern: Default SipHash for hot integer keys
antiMatrix.cause: Hashing dominates tiny lookups.
antiMatrix.fix: Faster hasher (`ahash`, `fxhash`) when keys are trusted.

antiMatrix.cause: Layout assumptions break: UB.
antiMatrix.fix: Safe conversions, `from_ne_bytes`, `bytemuck`.

antiMatrix.cause: Reading uninitialised memory is UB.
antiMatrix.fix: `MaybeUninit`.

antiMatrix.cause: Violates the aliasing rules: UB the optimiser exploits.
antiMatrix.fix: `UnsafeCell`, `Cell`, or redesign.

antiMatrix.cause: Layout mismatch and null derefs corrupt memory.
antiMatrix.fix: `repr(C)`, validate inputs, wrap in a safe API.

antiMatrix.pattern: Public fields on types with invariants
antiMatrix.cause: Callers can build invalid values.
antiMatrix.fix: Private fields plus constructors.

antiMatrix.cause: Adding a variant is a breaking change.
antiMatrix.fix: Mark the enum `#[non_exhaustive]`.

antiMatrix.cause: Monomorphisation bloats binaries and compile time.
antiMatrix.fix: Use `dyn` or concrete types where speed does not matter.

antiMatrix.cause: Supply-chain and licence risk.
antiMatrix.fix: `cargo audit`, `cargo deny`, review new crates, commit `Cargo.lock`.

antiMatrix.pattern: Ignoring clippy warnings, no CI gates
antiMatrix.cause: Style drift and real bugs reach main.
antiMatrix.fix: Run `fmt` and `clippy -D warnings` in CI.

scenarios.title: Memory Grows Steadily Until the Container Is OOM-Killed
scenarios.question: A Rust service's resident memory climbs by a few MB per hour. It restarts every night when Kubernetes kills it for exceeding its limit. There is no garbage collector, so what leaks and how do you find it?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Confirm the shape.** Graph RSS over time. A staircase that tracks traffic suggests a cache or queue; a smooth ramp suggests a leak per request.
2. **Check the usual suspects.** `Arc`/`Rc` cycles (parent holds child, child holds parent: use `Weak` for the back edge), `HashMap`s used as caches with no eviction or TTL, unbounded channels, `Box::leak`, tasks that never finish, and `mem::forget`.
3. **Profile allocations.** Run a staging build with `heaptrack`, `dhat` or the allocator's profiler (jemalloc `prof`) and diff two snapshots taken an hour apart; the growing call site is the culprit.
4. **Rule out the allocator.** Memory freed by Rust may be held by the allocator. Compare `malloc_stats` / jemalloc stats with RSS; try `MALLOC_CONF` decay settings or switch allocator.
5. **Fix and guard.** Bound every cache (LRU with a maximum size and TTL), use bounded channels, break cycles with `Weak`, add a memory metric and an alert at 80% of the limit.

scenarios.title: Latency Spikes Under Load but CPU Looks Idle
scenarios.question: An async API answers in 5 ms normally, but at 200 requests per second p99 jumps to seconds while CPU is only 30%. What is happening?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Suspect runtime starvation.** Tokio has a small number of worker threads; a handler that blocks (`std::thread::sleep`, synchronous DB or file I/O, heavy CPU, a held `std::sync::Mutex`) pins a worker so other tasks wait to be polled.
2. **Look with `tokio-console`.** It shows tasks with long poll times and tasks that are idle but never woken.
3. **Find the blocking call.** Search for synchronous crates in async code (blocking HTTP clients, `std::fs`, `reqwest::blocking`, `diesel` without a pool wrapper).
4. **Fix.** Move CPU or blocking work to `spawn_blocking` or `rayon`, replace with async equivalents, shorten critical sections, and set per-request timeouts.
5. **Prevent.** Add a runtime health metric (tokio-metrics: poll duration, queue depth) and a load test to CI.

scenarios.title: Requests Hang Forever and CPU Is at Zero
scenarios.question: After a deploy, some requests never complete. Threads and tasks exist but nothing progresses. How do you diagnose and fix a Rust deadlock?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Capture state.** Attach `gdb`/`lldb` (`thread apply all bt`) or send a signal that dumps backtraces; for async, use `tokio-console` to see tasks that are never woken.
2. **Read the pattern.** Two threads blocked in `Mutex::lock` on different locks is classic lock-order inversion; one thread locking the same non-reentrant mutex twice self-deadlocks; a `MutexGuard` held across `.await` makes another task wait for a lock whose owner is parked.
3. **Fix lock order** (always acquire in one global order or merge the locks), **shorten critical sections**, never hold a guard across `.await`, and avoid calling unknown callbacks while locked.
4. **Consider design changes**: message passing with an owner task, or `try_lock` with backoff.
5. **Defend.** Use `parking_lot` deadlock detection in staging and add timeouts so hangs turn into errors.

scenarios.title: One CPU Core at 100% and Throughput Is Capped
scenarios.question: A service uses 100% of a single core and cannot scale. Where do you look?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Profile, do not guess.** `perf record -g` or `cargo flamegraph` on a release build with debug symbols shows which functions dominate.
2. **Typical causes.** A regex with catastrophic backtracking (use the `regex` crate, which avoids it, or check the pattern), JSON (de)serialisation of large payloads on the hot path, a spin loop or busy `try_recv`, per-request allocation, logging at debug level, or all work funnelled through one task or lock.
3. **Fix the hot spot**: reuse buffers, borrow instead of clone, stream rather than load whole documents, move work to a pool.
4. **Scale the shape**: shard work across tasks/threads, use `rayon` for data parallelism, or run multiple processes behind a load balancer.
5. **Lock it in** with a criterion benchmark so the regression cannot return.

scenarios.title: A Panic Takes Down the Service
scenarios.question: A single malformed request triggers `unwrap()` on `None` and the process exits, dropping every in-flight request. How do you stop one bad input from killing everything?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Understand panic behaviour.** In a Tokio task a panic is caught at the task boundary (the `JoinHandle` returns `Err`), but in the main thread, in `panic = "abort"` builds, or in code you spawned on plain threads it can end the process.
2. **Fix the root cause**: replace `unwrap`/indexing on external data with `?`, `get`, validation and typed errors.
3. **Contain failures**: handle each request in its own task, log `JoinError`s, add a panic hook that records the backtrace and request id, and (for web frameworks) use a catch-panic middleware that turns it into a 500.
4. **Keep the service up**: run several replicas, add readiness probes, and use a supervisor (systemd, Kubernetes) with backoff.
5. **Prevent regressions** with fuzzing (`cargo fuzz`) or property tests (`proptest`) on parsers and handlers.

scenarios.title: OOM From a Growing Queue
scenarios.question: A consumer reads from Kafka and pushes work into an in-memory channel; under a traffic burst the process is OOM-killed. Why, and how do you fix it?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Diagnose.** The channel is unbounded (or very large) and the workers are slower than the intake, so messages pile up. Memory graphs track queue length.
2. **Add back-pressure.** Replace it with a bounded channel (`mpsc::channel(N)`); when full, the producer awaits, which slows the Kafka poll loop instead of exhausting RAM.
3. **Size correctly.** Bound by bytes rather than count if messages vary widely; use a `Semaphore` for in-flight work.
4. **Scale the consumers.** More partitions and consumers, concurrent workers per message batch, batching writes.
5. **Observe.** Export queue depth, consumer lag and processing time; alert on sustained growth.

scenarios.title: Database Pool Exhausted
scenarios.question: Requests fail with "timed out waiting for a connection from the pool" during peak traffic even though the database is healthy. What do you check?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Who holds connections?** A connection is returned only when its handle is dropped. Look for handlers that hold a connection (or an open transaction) across slow work such as HTTP calls or `sleep`.
2. **Check pool settings.** `max_connections` too low for concurrency, or so high that the database refuses them; set `acquire_timeout` so failures are fast and visible.
3. **Find slow queries.** Missing indexes make each connection busy longer; use the database's slow-query log and `EXPLAIN`.
4. **Fix.** Acquire late and release early, keep transactions short, add indexes, cache hot reads, and size the pool from database capacity divided by the number of instances.
5. **Monitor** pool wait time, active connections and query latency per route.

scenarios.title: Builds and CI Take 25 Minutes
scenarios.question: Developers wait 25 minutes for CI and several minutes for incremental builds. How do you speed up a Rust project?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Measure.** `cargo build --timings` shows which crates dominate; `cargo tree -d` shows duplicate dependency versions.
2. **Cache in CI** (`Swatinem/rust-cache`, sccache) and use `--locked`; build once and reuse artifacts between jobs.
3. **Reduce work.** Split the project into a workspace so unchanged crates are not rebuilt, trim heavy default features, prefer `dyn` over deep generics in hot compile paths, and avoid proc-macro-heavy dependencies where possible.
4. **Faster tooling.** Use `mold` or `lld` as the linker, `cargo nextest` for test runs, `cargo check` during development, and lower debug info for dev profiles.
5. **Right-size the pipeline**: run format and clippy in parallel with tests, and build release artifacts only on main.

scenarios.title: Rare Crashes or Corrupt Data From FFI or `unsafe` Code
scenarios.question: A service that wraps a C library crashes once a day with a segmentation fault, and sometimes returns garbage. How do you find undefined behaviour?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Get evidence.** Enable core dumps (`ulimit -c unlimited`), keep debug symbols, and read the backtrace with `gdb`/`lldb` to see whether the crash is in Rust or in C.
2. **Review the boundary.** Check `#[repr(C)]` layouts, ownership of every pointer (who frees what, with which allocator), nullability, string encoding (NUL-terminated `CString`), lifetimes of buffers passed to C, thread-safety of the C library, and that no panic unwinds into C.
3. **Run the tools.** Miri for the Rust side, AddressSanitizer/ThreadSanitizer (`RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=address` on nightly), and Valgrind for the C side.
4. **Shrink the unsafe surface**: one small module, a safe wrapper type that owns the pointer (`Drop` frees it) and exposes only checked operations.
5. **Add tests**: fuzz the wrapper API and run it under sanitizers in CI.

scenarios.title: Tail Latency Regressed After a Release
scenarios.question: After deploying a new version p99 latency doubled, but averages look the same. How do you find and remove the regression safely?
scenarios.answer:
1. **Contain first.** Roll back or shift traffic away from the new version (canary or blue-green), then investigate with less pressure.
2. **Compare versions.** Diff dependency updates (`Cargo.lock`), feature flags and config. Compare traces and flamegraphs from old and new builds under the same load.
3. **Look at the tail.** Lock contention, a new synchronous call, extra allocation per request, a changed timeout or retry policy, or a downstream that now gets more calls.
4. **Reproduce** with a load test (`k6`, `oha`, `wrk`) against a staging environment and bisect commits (`git bisect`) with a benchmark as the test.
5. **Fix and protect**: add the benchmark to CI with a threshold, keep canary rollout with automatic rollback on latency or error-rate alerts, and write the findings into the runbook.

## Production Scenario Matrix (11-30)

| # | Symptom / Alert | Root Cause Diagnostics | Immediate Remediation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **11** | `Too many open files` (EMFILE) | File or socket handles not dropped; a new HTTP client created per request. | `lsof -p <pid>`; share one `reqwest::Client`; drop handles; raise `ulimit -n`. |
| **12** | Requests hang with no error | Missing timeouts on network calls. | Wrap calls in `timeout`, set client connect and request timeouts. |
| **13** | Tokio workers at 100% but throughput low | CPU-bound work running on the async runtime. | Move it to `spawn_blocking` or `rayon`. |
| **14** | `already borrowed: BorrowMutError` panic | Overlapping `RefCell` borrows. | Shorten borrow scopes, restructure, or use `try_borrow_mut`. |
| **15** | Build error: future cannot be sent between threads | A non-`Send` value (`Rc`, `MutexGuard`) lives across `.await`. | Drop it before awaiting, switch to `Arc`, or use an async-aware lock. |
| **16** | Release binary is huge | Debug info, no LTO, large generic instantiations. | `strip = true`, `lto`, `opt-level = "s"`, `codegen-units = 1`. |
| **17** | Docker image is hundreds of MB | Single-stage build ships the toolchain. | Multi-stage build; copy the binary to distroless or scratch. |
| **18** | Linking errors with musl or OpenSSL | Dynamic OpenSSL not available for the target. | Use `rustls`, or vendor OpenSSL. |
| **19** | Periodic latency spikes | Lock contention or allocator behaviour under load. | Profile, shorten locks, try `mimalloc` or `jemalloc`. |
| **20** | Memory not returned to the OS | Allocator keeps freed pages cached. | Tune the allocator's decay settings; confirm with allocator stats. |
| **21** | Deserialisation errors right after a deploy | Strict schema changed between producer and consumer. | `#[serde(default)]`, tolerate unknown fields, version the schema. |
| **22** | Consumer lag keeps growing | Slow handler or single-threaded processing. | Batch work, add concurrency, add partitions and consumers. |
| **23** | Messages processed twice | At-least-once delivery without idempotency. | Idempotency keys or a dedup table; commit offsets after success. |
| **24** | "Works on my machine" builds differ | `Cargo.lock` not committed or ignored in CI. | Commit the lockfile and build with `--locked`. |
| **25** | Security advisory for a dependency | Outdated crate with a known CVE. | `cargo audit`, update or replace the crate, add `cargo deny` to CI. |
| **26** | Flaky tests | Shared global state, fixed ports, real time. | Isolate state, use temp dirs and port 0, `tokio::time::pause`. |
| **27** | Memory per connection is high | Large per-task buffers or futures. | Size buffers, box large futures, cap concurrency with a `Semaphore`. |
| **28** | Deploys drop in-flight requests | No graceful shutdown. | Handle SIGTERM and drain with `with_graceful_shutdown`. |
| **29** | Slow startup / failing readiness probes | Heavy initialisation before listening. | Lazy-init non-critical parts, parallelise startup, tune probe delays. |
| **30** | No metrics or traces in production | Service not instrumented. | Add `tracing` spans, Prometheus metrics, health and readiness endpoints. |
